body:
What is a flood?

A flood occurs when water covers land that is normally dry. In a river flood, the volume of water flowing through a river exceeds the capacity of its channel, and the excess water spreads into adjoining areas. Flooding can also occur when intense rainfall accumulates in a town or city faster than it can drain away.

Flooding is a natural hydrological process, but it becomes a disaster when it causes serious losses to people, property, livelihoods or essential services. The amount of damage depends not only on the quantity of water but also on the exposure and vulnerability of the affected population.

Three important forms of flooding

TypePrincipal mechanismDistinctive feature
River or riverine floodRiver discharge exceeds channel capacity and water spreads over adjoining land.May develop after prolonged or widespread rainfall in the upstream basin.
Flash floodWater rises or moves rapidly after intense rainfall or another sudden release of water.Short warning time and potentially fast, dangerous flow.
Urban floodRainwater accumulates where surface runoff exceeds the capacity of urban drainage or natural outlets.Can occur without a nearby river overflowing.

These categories can overlap. Intense rainfall may produce a flash flood in a small stream and simultaneously flood nearby urban streets. A city situated beside a major river can experience both riverine flooding and local drainage flooding.

How rainfall becomes floodwater

A drainage basin, also called a catchment, is the area from which rainfall and other water flow towards a common river or outlet. Its boundary is generally formed by higher land that separates one drainage system from another.

When rain falls, some water infiltrates the soil, some may be temporarily stored in vegetation or depressions, and the remainder flows over the surface as runoff. Infiltrated water may also reach streams later through subsurface pathways.

Flood risk becomes greater when intense rainfall supplies water faster than the catchment can absorb, store or convey it. Important influences include:

  • Rainfall intensity and duration: Very heavy rainfall over a short period can generate rapid runoff, while prolonged rain can saturate a large catchment.
  • Antecedent soil moisture: Already wet soil generally has less remaining capacity to absorb additional rainfall.
  • Slope: Steep terrain can concentrate runoff quickly and increase the speed of floodwater.
  • Vegetation and land cover: Vegetation can intercept rain, support infiltration and slow surface flow; removal of vegetation may increase runoff and erosion.
  • Channel and floodplain conditions: Obstructions, encroachment and altered drainage pathways can worsen flooding.

Floodplains, natural levees and sediment

A floodplain is the relatively flat land adjoining a river that has been shaped by river erosion and deposition and may be inundated during high flows. When a river overflows, its velocity often decreases away from the main channel, allowing sediment to settle. Repeated deposits can contribute to fertile alluvial soils.

Coarser sediment deposited close to the channel may gradually form raised natural banks called natural levees. These should not be confused with artificial embankments, which are constructed flood-protection structures. Neither a natural levee nor an artificial embankment makes all surrounding land permanently flood-free.

Floodplain fertility and flood risk are connected. Periodic deposition of sediment may benefit agriculture, but the same land remains exposed to inundation. Fertile soil is not evidence that construction on the floodplain is safe.

Why floods also occur in relatively dry regions

Low average annual rainfall does not guarantee freedom from floods. A dry region may receive unusually intense rain over a short period. Hard or dry soil surfaces, sparse vegetation, steep local slopes and restricted channels can then contribute to sudden runoff. In some circumstances, intense rainfall following a prolonged dry period produces flash floods even though the region is generally drought-prone.

This distinction matters in Gujarat. Kachchh and parts of northern Gujarat face substantial drought risk, yet intense rainfall can also produce flash flooding. Other parts of the state have important river systems, including the Narmada, Tapi, Mahi and Sabarmati, where upstream rainfall and river conditions influence downstream flood risk.

Prelims focus

  • Riverine flooding occurs when water exceeds a river channel's carrying capacity.
  • Flash floods are distinguished primarily by their rapid onset, not by a particular river size.
  • Urban flooding can occur independently of river overflow.
  • A drainage basin is the area contributing water to a common outlet.
  • Floodplains are associated with river deposition and periodic inundation.
  • Trap: A drought-prone region can also experience a destructive flash flood.

[Sources: NCERT, India: Physical Environment, Class 11, 2026–27, Chapter 6, Natural Hazards and Disasters, pp. 60–63; NCERT, Our Environment, Class 7, Chapter 3, Our Changing Earth, printed p. 15, 2018–19 reprint.]

body:
Why urbanisation changes the movement of rainwater

When land is covered with roads, roofs, concrete and other impervious surfaces, less rainwater can infiltrate directly into the ground. A greater proportion may therefore become surface runoff. Water reaches low-lying streets and drainage channels more quickly, increasing the possibility that they will be overwhelmed during a heavy shower.

Urban flooding is not simply the result of unusually heavy rainfall. The arrangement and condition of the city's drainage system also matter. A locality with blocked outlets or extensive construction in natural drainage paths may flood during rainfall that another locality can manage.

The principal causes of urban waterlogging

  • Loss of permeable land: Paving and building reduce opportunities for infiltration and temporary surface storage.
  • Obstruction of natural drains: Construction across streams, small channels and traditional drainage routes can prevent water from reaching its outlet.
  • Insufficient stormwater drainage: Drains may be unable to carry the runoff generated by a particular rainfall event.
  • Poor maintenance: Silt, litter and solid waste reduce the effective capacity of drains.
  • Loss of lakes, ponds and wetlands: Filling these water bodies removes spaces that formerly held stormwater.
  • Low-lying development: Buildings and roads placed in depressions or flood-prone areas remain exposed to accumulated water.

Stormwater drains and sewers are not identical. Stormwater drains are intended to convey rainwater. Sewers carry wastewater. Where sewage or solid waste enters stormwater channels, blockages and contamination can aggravate flooding. Some cities also have combined drainage arrangements, so the actual system must be understood locally.

Understanding the urban runoff pathway

Consider 2 neighbouring areas receiving the same intense rainfall. One has substantial open soil, trees, a pond and maintained drainage channels. The other has paved open spaces, a filled-in pond and drains blocked by waste. The second area is more likely to experience rapid surface runoff and local waterlogging, although the precise outcome also depends on rainfall, soil, slope and outlet conditions.

Floodplain management and land-use planning

Floodplain management reduces risk by controlling how land exposed to river flooding is used. It may include identifying areas likely to be inundated, protecting natural drainage channels, restricting highly vulnerable development and preserving space for floodwater.

Floodplain zoning is a land-use approach in which different activities are permitted or restricted according to their flood exposure. For example, preserving an exposed floodplain as open space may reduce the number of people and buildings placed in danger. Zoning does not prevent a flood from occurring; it reduces potential losses.

Embankments, drainage channels and reservoirs can help manage particular flood conditions, but physical structures have limitations. Unusually large flows, blocked outlets or inadequate maintenance can still produce flooding. A sound approach combines infrastructure with land-use planning, forecasts, public information and preparedness.

The sponge-city approach

A sponge city uses a combination of natural features and suitable urban infrastructure to absorb, temporarily store, slow, clean or reuse rainwater rather than allowing all of it to rush immediately into drains.

The underlying principle is to manage part of the rainfall close to where it falls. This reduces pressure on conventional stormwater channels and can provide environmental benefits.

MeasureHow it worksMain contribution
Rain gardenA planted, permeable depression receives runoff from nearby hard surfaces.Slows runoff and supports infiltration where ground conditions permit.
Permeable pavementAllows some water to pass through the paved surface into an appropriate underlying layer.Reduces direct surface runoff.
Urban pond or wetlandProvides space to hold and gradually release or retain water.Temporary storage and reduced pressure on outlets.
Detention pondTemporarily holds stormwater before releasing it gradually.Reduces the peak rate of runoff reaching downstream drains.
Rainwater harvestingCollects water from suitable surfaces for storage or managed recharge.Reduces immediate runoff and may conserve water for later use.

Detention mainly delays the release of water. Retention involves holding water, sometimes in a permanent pool or for subsequent use. The terms are related but not interchangeable.

Sponge-city measures are not substitutes for functional major drains or safe river outlets. Their effectiveness depends on local soils, groundwater conditions, available space, maintenance and rainfall intensity. For example, infiltration may become limited when soil is already saturated.

Application to Gujarat's cities

Urban centres such as Ahmedabad and Surat must manage rainfall alongside existing roads, buildings, water bodies and drainage channels. Relevant preventive measures include maintaining stormwater outlets, conserving natural drains, protecting low-lying storage spaces and keeping new construction out of identified high-risk locations.

These measures must be planned for the individual urban catchment. A rain garden or a new drain in one neighbourhood cannot independently solve a downstream obstruction affecting the wider drainage network.

Prelims focus

  • Impervious surfaces generally increase and accelerate surface runoff.
  • Encroachment on natural drainage routes can increase urban flood risk.
  • Floodplain zoning regulates land use to reduce potential flood damage.
  • Rain gardens, permeable surfaces and wetlands are examples of sponge-city measures.
  • Detention delays runoff; retention holds water for longer or for later use.
  • Trap: Urban flooding does not require a river to overflow.

[Sources: National Disaster Management Authority, National Disaster Management Guidelines: Management of Urban Flooding, September 2010, sections 1.2, 1.6, 4.12–4.20 and 4.23; NCERT, Resources and Development, Class 8, Chapter 2, Land, Soil, Water, Natural Vegetation and Wildlife Resources, printed pp. 14–17, 2018–19 reprint; NCERT, India: Physical Environment, Class 11, 2026–27, Chapter 6, pp. 60–63.]

title: Urban Flood Risk: Impervious Surfaces, Blocked Drains and Sponge-City Measures

body:
Why forecasting and warning are different

A forecast estimates the likely future condition of rainfall, river flow or water level using available observations and scientific methods. A warning communicates the possibility or expected severity of danger so that authorities and the public can act.

A forecast is not a guarantee. The reliability of an estimate depends on observations, rainfall predictions, catchment conditions and the time available before flooding. Flash floods are particularly difficult because water can rise rapidly and leave very little warning time.

Institutional responsibilities in India

InstitutionPrincipal roleInformation or action
India Meteorological Department (IMD)Observes and forecasts weather and rainfall.Heavy-rainfall warnings and quantitative precipitation forecasts.
Central Water Commission (CWC)Monitors and forecasts river and reservoir-related flood conditions.Flood-level forecasts and reservoir-inflow forecasts.
State and district authoritiesCoordinate disaster preparedness and protective action.Local warnings, evacuation decisions, shelters and relief coordination.
Urban local bodiesManage local drainage and urban flood preparedness.Drain maintenance, removal of obstructions and local public information.

Rainfall forecast, river-level forecast and inflow forecast

A quantitative precipitation forecast estimates how much rain may fall over an area during a stated period. It is a meteorological input. A river-level forecast estimates the water level at a river location, helping identify areas threatened by inundation. A reservoir-inflow forecast estimates water expected to enter a reservoir, assisting those responsible for its operation.

These products answer different questions. Heavy rainfall upstream does not automatically mean that every downstream location will flood; the resulting river level depends on the basin, existing storage, routing of water and other conditions.

Gujarat connection

IMD's Flood Meteorological Office at Ahmedabad provides meteorological support for flood forecasting on the Narmada, Tapi, Mahi, Sabarmati, Banas and Daman Ganga river systems. This is an example of coordination between meteorological services and river forecasting rather than a separate forecasting responsibility for every institution.

What reservoirs can and cannot do

A reservoir can store a portion of incoming river water and, under suitable conditions, reduce the peak flow passing downstream. This capacity is important because monsoon water is also needed for irrigation, drinking-water supply and other uses during drier months.

There is therefore a basic management balance between conserving water for later use and retaining sufficient space to receive high inflows. Space available for temporarily storing floodwater is commonly described as a flood cushion.

Reservoirs cannot prevent every flood. When inflows are exceptionally high or available storage is limited, downstream releases may be necessary. Such releases can contribute to downstream flooding, particularly if local rivers are already high. Timely forecasts, monitoring and communication are therefore essential.

A dam does not make downstream land flood-proof. Its effect depends on storage availability, incoming water, operating conditions and the downstream river system.

Structural and non-structural flood-risk measures

Flood-risk measures are often grouped into 2 broad categories:

  • Structural measures: Physical works such as embankments, reservoirs, drainage improvements and appropriately designed flood-protection infrastructure.
  • Non-structural measures: Floodplain zoning, risk mapping, forecasting, warnings, public education, evacuation planning and protection of natural drainage.

The categories complement each other. For instance, an embankment may reduce the frequency of inundation in one area, while a warning system is still needed because overtopping or other failures remain possible.

Standard precautions before and during flooding

People in flood-prone settlements should know nearby safe elevated areas, likely routes to safety and official warning channels. Important documents, essential medicines, drinking water and basic necessities should be kept accessible when severe flooding is anticipated.

During flooding, the public should follow official evacuation instructions and avoid entering moving or unknown-depth floodwater. Flooded roads may conceal open drains, damaged surfaces or strong currents. People should not drive through flooded roads or approach fallen electrical wires or submerged electrical equipment.

After floodwater recedes, safe drinking water and hygiene are important because contaminated water may spread disease. Buildings and electrical systems affected by flooding should not be assumed safe merely because the visible water has disappeared.

Prelims focus

  • IMD provides meteorological observations and rainfall forecasts.
  • CWC provides river-level and reservoir-inflow forecasts.
  • Level forecasts support decisions about flood exposure and evacuation.
  • Inflow forecasts assist reservoir operations.
  • Floodplain zoning and public warnings are non-structural measures.
  • Trap: A reservoir may moderate flooding, but it cannot guarantee that downstream flooding will never occur.

[Sources: IMD, Hydrometeorological Services in IMD, sections Flood Meteorological Offices and Flood Meteorological Service, consulted 2 November 2026; Central Water Commission, Flood Management in India: A Statistical Report–2023, published July 2024, Chapter 3, Flood Forecasting; NDMA, National Disaster Management Guidelines: Management of Urban Flooding, September 2010, Chapters 3–5; NCERT, India: Physical Environment, Class 11, 2026–27, Chapter 6, pp. 62–63.]
